title: In situ STEM-EELS Study of Nitride Film Based Resistive Switching Device
content: Understanding the resistive switching (RS) mechanisms in different types of microelectronic devices is a critical step in the development of next-generation energy-efficient memory and computing units. Over the past decade, numerous studies on various metal-insulator-metal (MIM) structures have revealed the filament-type RS mechanism, namely the formation and rupture of conductive channels that lead to the low resistance state (LRS) and high resistance state (HRS) of the device. Yet, the filament-type RS devices usually suffer from undesirable temporal and spatial variations due to the random formation/rupture of the conductive filaments. In contrast, another interface-type RS devices whose resistive state is dominated by the semiconductor (or insulator) and metal interfaces, exhibit lower threshold switching voltage and more reliable switching repeatability, thus showing great promise in data storage memory and neuromorphic computing [1, 2]. Several different models have been proposed to explain the interface-type switching mechanisms, such as charge carriers (i.e. hole or electron) trapping and/or detrapping, electrochemical migration of oxygen vacancies, and even Mott transition induced by carriers doped at the interface [3-5]. However, due to the limited materials examples and challenges for implementing in situ characterization experiments, the RS mechanisms of interface-type RS devices are much less studied, which undoubtedly hinders their potential applications.
